en: The *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, translated from the Kāśyapīya school by the Uighur Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci:
This *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* is difficult to hear even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
To embrace and practice correctly—this matter is doubly difficult.
The arising of a Buddha in the world is joy; his teaching the Dharma upon arising in the world is joy.
The harmony of the Saṃgha is joy; maintaining the precepts in harmony is joy.
"Venerable sirs!

One month has passed and three months remain; old age and death are approaching, and the Buddha-dharma is gradually fading away. You should practice with single-minded diligence and not act with negligence."

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, through diligent and energetic effort, attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, as well as other wholesome dharmas and factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
"The Sangha is assembled in harmony;
let those who have not yet received full ordination depart.
"What should the harmoniously assembled Sangha do first?"
The bhikṣus who did not come have declared their *chanda* and purity.
Which bhikṣuṇī has been sent to receive the instruction?
“Vipaśyin Tathāgata, [attended by] six million eight hundred thousand [monks].”
Among the assembly of Arhats, he proclaimed these precepts of liberation:
"Patience is the supreme principle; the Buddha declared Nirvana to be foremost.
One who causes distress to others while claiming to have left the home life is not called a śramaṇa."
The Honored Muni Śikhin, a golden mountain beyond compare,
To an assembly of three hundred and sixty thousand, Proclaimed these precepts of liberation:
"Just as a person with clear vision, Being possessed of feet, can avoid treacherous terrain."
In this world there are wise people who are able to distance themselves from all calamities.
The Tathāgata Viśvabhū, forever free from all afflictions,
proclaimed these precepts of liberation amidst an assembly of hundreds of thousands:
Do not speak of others' faults in private; do not trouble or disturb others.
Constantly practice the precepts, knowing moderation and contentment in food and clothing.
Krukanṭa Buddha possessed vast knowledge and vision and was free from fear.
Within an assembly of forty thousand, he proclaimed these precepts of liberation:
"Just as a bee gathers from flowers, taking only their fragrance and flavor,
and carries them to its dwelling place;"
Not violating the intentions of others, One does not observe what is done or left undone;
Rather, one observes only one’s own bodily conduct, Whether it be right or wrong.
Kanakamuni, with thirty thousand śramaṇas—
Within the great assembly of Arhats, he preached this precept of liberation:
"Observe correctly and do not be negligent; you should train in the Dharma of the Muni.
Thus, free from sorrow and grief, with a tranquil mind, enter Nirvana."
The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, of great wisdom and great renown, amidst an assembly of thirty thousand, proclaimed this code of liberation:
"Commit no evil whatsoever; cultivate all that is wholesome."
To discipline one's own mind— this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
The World-Honored One of Great Wisdom, the Muni, the Dharma King Śākya,
for the sake of the Nairayika assembly, proclaimed these precepts of liberation:
Guard well your verbal karma, purify your own mind and intentions, and commit no evil with the body; these three karmas are thus purified.
The Saṃgha is exceedingly vast, and the teaching of the Dharma is likewise immeasurable.
"Renowned and receiving great offerings, he shall preach this Prātimokṣa.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha holds the uposatha and recites the Prātimokṣa."
"If the Sangha has arrived, may the Sangha listen with patience; the Sangha shall perform the *poṣadha* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*.
Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable sirs!..."
Now I shall proclaim the Prātimokṣa; you who have assembled, listen in silence and reflect upon it well.
Those who have committed an offense should confess it; those who have not committed an offense may remain silent.
Because of their silence, it is known that the assembly is pure.

Just as each individual bhikṣu is questioned, so too is the bhikṣu questioned up to three times. If, when questioned thus within the assembly up to three times, a bhikṣu remembers having committed an offense, he should confess it; if he does not confess it, he incurs the guilt of a deliberate falsehood.
Venerable sirs, the Blessed One has declared that the offense of intentional lying is an obstacle to the path.
If a bhikṣu recalls having committed such an offense and desires to seek purification, he should disclose it.
To disclose [one's offenses] brings peace and security; not to disclose them makes the offense deeper.
Venerable sirs!
I have finished reciting the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
"Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter?
Thus he asks three times. "The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter, for they are silent; thus it shall be held."
"Venerable sirs!
These four *pārājika* dharmas are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

If a bhikṣu, having entered the same dharma of precepts as other bhikṣus, while his precepts are weak and he has not renounced them, commits an impure act by practicing the way of sexual desire—even with an animal—this bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense and should not live in community."
"If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes the property of another that has not been given, with a mind of theft—
whether a king or a high minister should seize him, harm him, bind him, fine him, expel him from the country, or inflict various sufferings upon him, saying: 'Hey!'"
"You are a thief; you know nothing; you are deluded; you have taken what was not given.
If this monk is thus addressed, he commits a pārājika offense and should not live in communion.

"If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being or one who resembles a human being with his own hand—whether by personally wielding a blade, or by seeking out someone to wield a blade, or by instructing them to die, or praising death, saying: 'O man!'"
"What is the use of this unwholesome and evil life?
Death is better than life.

Following whatever that person desires and whatever they contemplate, he provides immeasurable and various instructions for death and praises of death; because of these matters, that person dies. This bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with others.
"If a bhikṣu, not knowing and not seeing the state of a superior person, lacking noble knowledge and vision of the sublime Dharma, should claim for himself:
'I know, I see.'"
At a later time, whether he is questioned or not questioned, desiring to be found pure, he speaks thus:
"I truly did not know and did not see, yet I said I knew and I saw; it was a false, deceptive, and lying speech."
"Excepting one who has overweening pride, this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not live in community. "Venerable sirs!
I have finished reciting the four pārājika dharmas."
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these offenses, he may not dwell together with the bhikṣus, just as those who have committed a pārājika offense previously may not dwell together.
Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it was said three times: "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent; thus shall this matter be held.
"Venerable sirs!"
These thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, except during a dream, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."

"If a bhikṣu, with a defiled mind, makes physical contact with a woman—whether grasping her hand, grasping her arm, grasping her hair, or touching any part of her body and experiencing the sensation of touch—it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣu, with a defiled mind, utters coarse and lewd words regarding sexual desire, as men and women might speak to one another, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"If a bhikṣu, in the presence of a woman, praises himself, saying:
'Sister! We uphold the precepts and well-cultivate the holy life; you should honor me with sexual desire, for this is the foremost offering of the Dharma.'"
“Saṃghāvaśeṣa.

‘If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between, conveying a man’s intent to a woman and conveying a woman’s intent to a man, whether for marriage or for illicit intercourse, even if only for a moment, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.’”
"If a bhikṣu seeks to have a dwelling built for himself, being the owner and building it for his own use, he must build it according to the prescribed measurements.
Herein, the measurements are: twelve spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and seven spans in internal width."
He should take other bhikṣus to inspect the site; those bhikṣus should examine the site to ensure it is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.

If a bhikṣu seeks to have a hut built for himself on a site with difficulties or obstructions, where there is no patron and he builds it for his own use, and if he does not take other bhikṣus to inspect the site or if he exceeds the prescribed dimensions, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
“If a bhikṣu wishes to have a large dwelling constructed for himself by a patron, he should take other bhikṣus to inspect the site.
Those bhikṣus should examine the site to ensure it is free from obstacles and free from encumbrances.”
If a bhikṣu, for the first time, prepares the ground to build a large dwelling for himself that has a patron, and does not take other bhikṣus along to inspect the site, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If a bhikṣu, out of malice, should defame a pure bhikṣu who is free from offense by means of groundless *pārājika* charges, desiring to destroy that bhikṣu’s pure conduct."
At a later time, whether he is questioned or rebuked, or even if he is not questioned, he says:
"This matter was spoken by me without basis; I spoke these words out of anger."

Saṃghāvaśeṣa: "If a bhikṣu, out of malice, slanders a pure and faultless bhikṣu with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense using a similar rule, for the purpose of destroying that person's holy life."
At another time, whether he is questioned or not questioned, it is known that this was a similar case belonging to a different category; the bhikṣu himself says:
"I spoke falsely out of anger."
Saṃghāvaśeṣa: "If a bhikṣu, desiring to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, adopts the methods for causing such a schism and persists in them without relinquishing them."
The monks should admonish that monk, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
do not persistently uphold and refuse to relinquish the practices that lead to a schism."

Venerable sir, may you live in harmony with the Saṅgha; may the Saṅgha be harmonious, joyful, and free from dispute; may they study under the same teacher as one, blending like water and milk, increasing their well-being and dwelling in peace.
"Venerable one!
Abandon this method of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus have admonished him in this manner, it is well if he abandons it;
If he does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it after up to three admonitions, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
“If a bhikkhu has other companion bhikkhus belonging to his faction—whether two, three, or even more—who speak in accordance with him, and they say to the bhikkhus:
‘Venerable sirs!...’”
"Do not admonish this bhikṣu; this bhikṣu has no evil intent. Why is this?

What this bhikṣu has spoken is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya. This bhikṣu speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge. What this bhikṣu has spoken is what our own hearts desire, find joy in, and accept."
"Whatever this bhikṣu desires, delights in, and accepts, I likewise desire,
delight in, and accept. The bhikṣus said,
"Venerable One!"
Do not speak these words:
"What this bhikkhu has spoken is in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya; this bhikkhu speaks knowingly and not unknowingly.
This bhikkhu delights in and approves of it, and I likewise delight in and approve of it."
Why is this? What this bhikṣu has spoken is neither Dharma nor Vinaya; this bhikṣu does not speak with knowledge, Venerable Sir!
Do not seek to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha!
Venerable one,
you should delight in harmony and remain in concord with the Saṃgha.

The Saṃgha is now in harmony, joyful, and without dispute; dwelling together and training under the same teacher, they are like water and milk mixed together, increasing in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma.
"Venerable ones!
Desist from this dispute that causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus have admonished them in this way, it is well if they desist.
If he does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"If there are bhikṣus who dwell in dependence upon villages or towns, who corrupt their lineage and engage in evil conduct—
such that their corruption of the lineage is seen, heard, and known, and their engagement in evil conduct is also seen, heard, and known."
The bhikṣus said to this bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!
You have defiled the lineage and committed evil deeds."
"It is seen, heard, and known that you have defiled your lineage; it is seen, heard, and known that you have engaged in evil conduct.
Venerable one!
You have defiled your lineage and have engaged in evil conduct."
"Go out, you; you should not remain here.
Those bhikṣus said to the other bhikṣus:
"The bhikṣus have attachment, they have aversion, they have delusion, and they have fear."
There may be other fellow bhikṣus who are expelled, while others are not.
Those bhikṣus should say to this bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!..."
Do not speak these words:
"The Saṃgha has favoritism, anger, delusion, and fear;
among the fellow bhikṣus practicing together, some are expelled while others are not."
Why is this? Because, Elder,
the bhikṣus are without attachment, without aversion, without delusion, and without fear.
"You have defiled the lineage; you have committed evil deeds.
That you have defiled the lineage is seen, heard, and known by us; that you have committed evil deeds is also seen, heard, and known."
"You defile the lineage and practice evil conduct; you must abandon these words characterized by lust, hatred, delusion, and fear.
When this bhikṣu is thus admonished, it is well if he abandons them;
if he does not abandon them, the other bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may abandon this matter.
Up to three admonitions, if he relinquishes [the behavior], it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

"If a bhikṣu speaks with harsh words, and when being instructed according to the Dharma and the Vinaya within the training of the precepts and the Dharma of the Tathāgata, he himself does not accept the admonition and says to the bhikṣus:..."
"Elder! Do not speak to me of what is wholesome or unwholesome; nor shall I speak to you elders of what is wholesome or unwholesome. Elders!"
"Stop! Do not admonish me.
The bhikṣus then admonished this bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable one!"
Training within the Buddha’s teachings of the precepts according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, you yourself should accept admonition and not refuse it.
Venerable sir,
as you admonish the bhikṣus according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, so too should the bhikṣus admonish you according to the Dharma and the Vinaya.
Why is this? Because when they are thus complete, the community of disciples of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, attains growth.
They admonish one another with various forms of counsel, instruct one another in turn, each repents of their faults, and each engages in mutual conversation.
When that bhikṣu has been thus admonished, it is well if he relinquishes [the matter];
if he does not relinquish it, the other bhikṣus should admonish him three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
Even unto the third admonition, it is well if he relinquishes it; [if he does not, he commits an offense].
"If one does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"Venerable sirs, I have finished reciting the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine are offenses upon the first commission, and four require up to three admonitions."
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these offenses and conceals it according to his knowledge, he should undergo the *parivāsa* (probation).
Having completed the *parivāsa*, he should undergo the *mānatva* (penance) for six nights within the Saṃgha.

Once the practitioner of humble conduct has completed the purification of his mind, he should be granted the removal of his offense; this requires the extinction of the offense within an assembly of twenty monks who act in accordance with the Dharma.
If there is one person short and the number does not reach twenty to extinguish the offense of this bhikṣu, the offense of that bhikṣu cannot be removed.
The bhikṣus may also have committed offenses;
such is the nature of this Dharma.
Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it was said three times: "Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent; thus shall this matter be upheld.
"Venerable sirs!"
These two indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharmas) are recited every half-month from within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra:
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place where no one can see them, and speaks of carnal desires."
If a faithful upāsikā speaks of each of these three matters—one by one—whether it be a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika offense.
The bhikṣu sitting in that place says of himself:
"I have committed this offense.
Among the three categories of dharma, he should be dealt with according to each one: whether it be a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika.
If what has been said by a trustworthy female lay follower is true, that bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
This is called an undetermined rule (aniyata-dharma).
"If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a woman..."
If a faithful upāsikā states one of two offenses— either a saṃghāvaśeṣa or a pāyattika—
and the bhikṣu sitting there says of himself,
"I have committed this offense," [it is a confession].
"Among these two categories of offenses, each should be dealt with accordingly—whether it be a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*.
If what has been said by a trustworthy female lay follower (*upāsikā*) is true, that bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma."
"These are called the indeterminate rules (aniyata-dharmas). Venerable sirs!
I have now recited the two indeterminate rules."
"Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter?
Thus he asks three times. "The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter, for they remain silent; thus it shall be held."
"Venerable sirs!
These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules are derived from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month.
'If a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished, he may keep an extra robe for up to ten days.'"
If one keeps [an extra robe] beyond that limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu, having finished making his robes and having the *kaṭhina* privileges withdrawn, stays apart from any one of his three robes in another place for even one night, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (*saṃgha-kamma*), it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having cast out the kaṭhina cloth, obtains an out-of-season robe, he may accept it if he needs it; having accepted it, he must quickly complete the robe."
If it is sufficient, it is well; if it is insufficient, one may keep it for up to one month.
If one keeps it longer than that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu exchanges a robe with a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or beat an old robe for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu begs for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
As for "other times": being deprived of one's robes, losing one's robes, having one's robes burned, or having one's robes carried away by water—these are called "other times.
"If a bhikṣu is deprived of his robes, loses his robes, has his robes burned, or has his robes carried away by water..."
If non-relatives, namely laymen or laywomen of faith, give many robes, that bhikṣu should receive them with moderation.
If he receives more than that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative prepares the price for a robe for that bhikṣu and gives this robe-price to a certain bhikṣu:..."
If that bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering, goes to the house of a layperson and speaks thus:
"Layperson, have you truly prepared the price for a robe for my sake?"
The householder said,
"It is indeed so.
The bhikṣu said:
"Excellent, householder!
You should prepare such fine-colored robes for me, because they are of good quality.
If he obtains the robes [in this manner], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, two householders each provide the price for a robe for that bhikṣu, saying:
'Once this item has been made into a robe, it shall be given to such-and-such a bhikṣu.'"
"Suppose that monk, without having previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering, remembers it and goes to the house of that layperson, saying: 'Layperson!
Do you two truly intend to make a robe for me?'"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The bhikṣu said:
"Excellent, householder!
You have prepared the price for such fine robes.
For my sake, let us together make one robe, so that it may be of good quality."
If he obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a monk, by a king, a great minister, a brahmin, a householder, a lay devotee, a merchant leader, or the wife of a householder, is sent the price for a robe with the instruction:
'Take this price for a robe and give it to such-and-such a monk.'"
That messenger went to where the bhikṣu was and spoke thus:
"Venerable sir!
Please accept this price for a robe out of compassion."
The bhikṣu said:
"I should not accept this price for robes.
When I have need of a robe, I shall accept it once I have obtained a pure robe."
The messenger said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
Are there any attendants?"
The bhikṣu who needs robes says:
"There is. Whether it be a park-keeper or an upāsaka, these are the attendants for the bhikṣus."
That messenger went to the person in charge and said: "Manager!
This is the price for robes for such-and-such a bhikṣu; having had the robes made for him, you shall give them to that bhikṣu at such-and-such a time."
After the messenger had delivered the price for the robe, he went to where the bhikṣu was and said to him:
"Venerable sir!
I have already given the price for the robe to the attendant designated by you."
"Venerable sir!
When you need robes, go and take them; you shall receive robes.
The bhikṣu who needs robes goes to the place where the attendant is and speaks to him two or three times:
"I require a robe.
If he succeeds in obtaining a robe after reminding [the donor] two or three times, that is well.
If he does not obtain a robe, he should stand silently before [the donor] four, five, or six times to cause him to remember.
If he stands silently before [the donor] four, five, or six times, it is well if he obtains the robe;
if he does not obtain the robe, and he obtains it by seeking beyond that number of times, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go himself or send a reliable messenger to the place from which the price for the robe originated, and say to the donor:
"The robe-price you previously sent by messenger to such-and-such a bhikṣu has not been received by that bhikṣu."
"The donor shall take it back; do not let it be lost.
This is called acting in accordance with the Dharma.
"If a bhikṣu makes a bedding out of silk (kauśeya) mixed [with other materials], or causes another to make one, and it is completed, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu makes a bedding out of pure black sheep’s wool, or causes another to make it, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).

If a bhikṣu makes a bedding, he should use two parts of black sheep’s wool, a third part of white, and a fourth part of variegated; if he causes another to make it, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he must take a piece of the old one measuring one cubit square and patch it onto the new one.
If he does not do so, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika)."
"If a bhikṣu makes a bedding mat, he should use it for six years.
If he makes another bedding mat before the six years have elapsed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣu obtains wool while traveling on a road, he may take it if he requires it.
If there is no one to carry it for him, he may carry it himself for a distance of three yojanas."
If he exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of trading of precious objects, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣu takes precious objects with his own hand, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl without having made it a formal gift (*apariśuddha-dāna*), and it exceeds ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu has an alms bowl that is less than five patches old and not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, and obtains one, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika."
That bhikṣu should relinquish it within the Saṃgha; if there is no other bhikṣu who possesses a bowl, he should accept it.
He should maintain it well until it breaks.
This rule should be thus.
"If a bhikṣu himself begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has a householder who is not a relative employ a weaver to weave a robe for him..."
This bhikṣu, having previously received no formal invitation, goes to the weaver’s place with mindfulness and says to the weaver:
"You should know now that this robe is being woven for me."
"Make it very well-woven and fine; I shall give you some price for the cloth.
If a bhikṣu gives the price—even as much as the cost of a single meal—and obtains the cloth, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger, either takes it back himself or causes another to take it back, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"If a bhikṣu, when less than ten days remain before the end of the three-month summer retreat, receives an urgent gift of robes (ātyayika-cīvara), he may accept it if he has need of it; having accepted it, he should keep it for the duration of the prescribed period."
If one keeps it beyond that period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, when there is one month remaining in the spring season, should seek a rain-bathing robe; he should use it after half a month has passed."
If one uses them beyond this limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣu is in a forest hermitage where there is suspicion or fear, he may leave any one of his three robes within a dwelling; furthermore, if there is a valid reason, he may go beyond the boundary and remain separated from his robe for up to six nights."
If he exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu knows that an object has been given to the Saṃgha..."
If one takes it back for oneself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu has an illness, he is permitted to keep ghee, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar; he may consume them for up to seven days."
"If one takes it for more than seven days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Venerable sirs,
I have now recited the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas."
"Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter?
Thus he asks three times. "The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter, for they are silent; thus I shall hold it to be so."
“Venerable sirs!
These ninety *pāyattika* dharmas come from the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, which is recited every half-month.
‘If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks a falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*.’”
"If a bhikṣu speaks with double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu speaks with disparaging words, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu reopens a legal matter that has been settled according to the Dharma by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except in the presence of a man capable of understanding, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu recites the scriptures together with one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, toward one who has not yet received full ordination, claims for himself that he has attained a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), even if it is true, it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (thullaccaya), speaks of it to one who has not received the higher ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (saṃghakamma), it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that an item has been offered by another for the Sangha, diverts it to give to an acquaintance, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu, during the fortnightly recitation of the precepts, should say:
'What is the use of these minor, trivial rules?'"
"If, when these precepts are being recited, one causes others to feel regret, distress, or doubt,
because of thus disparaging the precepts, it is a *pāyattika* offense. Ten."
"If a bhikṣu destroys the seed-villages of the spirits, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu reviles or scolds another, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu places monastic bedding in an open space and departs without either putting it away himself or instructing another to put it away, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu spreads grass or leaves within a monastic dwelling and departs without either putting them away himself or instructing another to put them away, he commits a pāyattika offense."

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already occupied a dwelling, later arrives and forcibly spreads out bedding to stay, saying: 'If you find it cramped, you should leave of your own accord.'"
For this reason, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, out of prior anger and for the sake of causing disturbance, drags another out of the room, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu sits or lies down upon a bed with removable legs on an upper story of a dwelling without providing support, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, pours it himself onto grass or soil, or instructs another to pour it, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu wishes to construct a large dwelling, he should personally inspect it for two or three layers of roofing up to the windows.
If he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika. Twenty."

In foreign countries, windows are opened on flat-roofed houses; after covering them crosswise with two or three boards, one reaches the casement. "If a bhikṣu, not appointed by the Saṃgha, teaches bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha, instructs bhikṣuṇīs until sunset, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu enters a bhikṣuṇī monastery and, for a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill, preaches the Dharma and provides instruction, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'The bhikṣus teach the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of material support,' it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a bhikṣuṇī, except for other times, it is a pāyattika.
'Other times' refers to when one travels with many companions or when there is suspicion and fear; these are the other times."
"If a bhikṣu travels on the same boat with a bhikṣuṇī, whether going upstream or downstream—except for a direct crossing—it is a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu eats food knowing that it was praised by a bhikṣuṇī, except when the donor had prior intention, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu eats in succession [at multiple locations], except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The 'appropriate times' are: when one is ill, when one is making robes, and when robes are being distributed; these are the appropriate times."
“If a monk, at a place where a single meal is offered, being free from illness, should eat only one meal.
If he receives more than that, it is a *pāyattika*.
“If many monks go to a donor’s house for alms, and a faithful and dharma-practicing elder gives them much rice and flour, the monks who require it should take two or three bowls.”
If one takes more than this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
One should carry it to one's dwelling and eat it together with others;
this is how the rule should be followed.
"If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal, eats again, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has finished his meal, invites him to eat, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, except at the appropriate times, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).

The 'appropriate times' are: when one is ill, when making robes, when robes are being distributed, when traveling on a road, when traveling by boat, during a great assembly, and when śramaṇas are distributing food; these are the appropriate times."
"If a bhikṣu eats solid or soft food at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu eats food that has been stored overnight, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, except for water and tooth-sticks, takes food that has not been offered and puts it into his mouth, it is a pāyattika.

"If a bhikṣu, when obtaining fine and delicious food—such as ghee, oil, honey, rock-honey, milk, curd, fresh butter, or fish or meat—seeks it for himself and eats it while not being ill, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, drinks or uses it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that it is a family’s mealtime, enters directly [without prior announcement], he commits a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣu sits insistently in a family home where a meal is being served, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a renunciant of a non-Buddhist sect, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu goes to view an army formation, except for a legitimate reason, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu, having a legitimate reason to enter an army, stays for more than two nights and reaches a third night, it is a pāyattika.”

"If a bhikṣu stays among an army for two or three nights and observes the military's mobilization, its strength, banners, and standards, watching various things with a mind of delight and compliance, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, with a mind of anger, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, with a mind of anger, makes a threatening gesture toward another bhikṣu with his hand, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, conceals it, he commits a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, having given his consent (chanda), later regrets it, he commits a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir!
Come together with me to such-and-such a village; I shall give you much delicious food.'"
When that bhikṣu arrived at the village, he did not give any food to this bhikṣu at all,
but said to him:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Go! I do not find pleasure in sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure in sitting and speaking alone.
If one sends another away for no other reason than this, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, without a cause or condition of illness, lights a fire in the open air or instructs another to light one, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a person who has not received full ordination for up to three nights, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu should speak thus:
'I know the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; practicing sexual intercourse does not obstruct the path,' the other bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu, saying:"
"Elder! Do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One, for to slander the World-Honored One is unwholesome.
The World-Honored One does not say such a thing. By means of countless skillful means, the World-Honored One has taught that engaging in sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path."
"Thus the Blessed One has declared that sensual desire obstructs the path; Elder, abandon this evil view.
If that bhikṣu abandons it when thus admonished, it is well.
If he does not abandon it, that bhikṣu should admonish him up to three times so that he may abandon that matter.
Up to three admonitions, if he relinquishes [the view], it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that such a person has not relinquished his evil view, stays with him, eats with him, or performs the same formal act (*karmavācanā*) as him, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has spoken thus:
'I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma to be such that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path.'"
The bhikṣus should admonish this śrāmaṇera, saying:
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One, for it is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One does not speak thus;
rather, the World-Honored One has taught by means of countless skillful methods that the practice of sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path."
"Śrāmaṇera!
Abandon this evil view.
If he abandons it when thus admonished, that is well.
If he does not relinquish it, that bhikṣu should say to this śrāmaṇera:
"From this day forward, you must no longer say, 'The World-Honored One is my Great Teacher.'"
"You do not conform to the holy life and may not follow along with the other bhikṣus.
As for other śrāmaṇeras, they are permitted to stay with great bhikṣus for two or three nights; you, foolish man, have no such privilege now."
"Go away and be extinguished; you need not stay here.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been thus expelled, should keep him as a co-resident or share a lodging with him, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu slanders another with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu uses a novice’s robe or bowl that has been offered as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dakṣiṇā*) without asking permission, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu travels along a road with a woman, even as far as the distance between two villages, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣu to feel troubled by doubt, even for a brief moment, such that he finds no pleasure, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu tickles a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu frightens another bhikṣu, even in jest, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣu hides another bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, or requisites, or instructs another to hide them—even in jest—with the exception of other [appropriate] times, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu obtains new cloth and does not dye it an unattractive color—blue, black, or madder—he commits a pāyattika offense.
“If a bhikṣu takes up a gem or what resembles a gem, either by himself or by instructing another to take it, he commits a pāyattika offense, except in the case of a monastery or a lodging.”
If one takes a precious ornament or decorative item with the thought,
"I shall return this," this is the proper occasion.
"If a bhikṣu bathes once every half-month, except during the special times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The special times are: the heat of summer, the time of illness, the time of manual labor, the time of wind, the time of rain, and the time of travel; these are the [permitted] times."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that one is a companion of bandits, travels together with them along the same road for even as far as the distance between two villages, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a person is less than twenty years of age, confers full ordination upon them, it is a pāyattika."
This person does not obtain the precepts, and the Saṃgha incurs an offense.
This rule is thus:
“If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for four months, a bhikṣu who is free from illness should accept it.”
If one accepts more than this—except in cases of a regular invitation, a repeated invitation, an invitation for a specific portion, or a lifelong invitation—it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth himself, or instructs another to dig the earth, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'You should train in this precept,' and that bhikṣu says:"
"I will not learn the precepts from you—a foolish person and one who speaks improperly—nor even hold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Mātṛkā. I shall instead inquire about the *pāyattika* offenses."
Those who seek understanding should question monks who uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā.
This is in accordance with the Dharma.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that others are engaged in a dispute, listens silently to these words and then reports them to those [involved], it is a pāyattika offense."
“If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is reciting the Prātimokṣa, departs in silence without having given his consent (chanda), it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣu is disrespectful, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣu has previously accepted an invitation, whether for a meal before or after the midday meal, he commits a pāyattika offense if he goes to another household without informing another bhikṣu.
"If a bhikṣu enters the palace gate while the consecrated king’s night has not yet ended and the king has not yet departed, except for a specific cause."
Pāyattika: "If a bhikṣu, when the Prātimokṣa is being recited, should speak thus:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"I have only now learned that this rule is recited in the Bi-monthly Precept Sūtra.
If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has already sat in the place where the precepts were recited two or three times previously, let alone for a longer period.
According to the offense committed by that bhikṣu, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma; furthermore, the method for increasing his sense of weary detachment should be applied:
"Venerable one!
You have gained no benefit and have acquired what is unwholesome."
"At the time of the recitation of the precepts, you did not listen with a single-minded focus, you were not respectful, you did not apply your attention, and you did not maintain mindfulness.
This is called "disgust," and it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu fashions a needle case out of bone, ivory, or horn, it is a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight fingers of the Tathāgata, excluding the portion inserted into the frame."
If it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu stores cotton-wool in a corded bed or a wooden bed, whether he makes it himself or instructs another to make it, if it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣu makes a sitting mat, he should make it according to the proper measure.
Herein, the measure is: two handspans in length by one and a half handspans in width; or, the width and length may each be increased by an additional half handspan."
If it exceeds these measurements, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a garment to cover scabies, he must make it according to the prescribed measure.
The measure herein is: four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width."
If it exceeds [the prescribed measure], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-cloak, he must make it according to the proper measure.
The measure therein is: six hands in length and two and a half hands in width."
If it is completed when exceeding [the measure], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to that of the Tathāgata, or makes a robe exceeding that size, and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*."
"Regarding the measurement of a Buddha’s robe among these: it is nine hand-spans in length and six hand-spans in width;
this is called the measurement of a Buddha’s robe. "Venerable sirs!"
"I have already explained the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas.
Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in regard to these matters?
Thus it is asked three times. "The Venerable Ones are pure in regard to these matters, for they remain silent; thus I shall hold this matter to be so."
"Venerable sirs!
These four dharmas of confession originate from the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month.
'If a bhikṣu enters a village to beg for food and, being without illness, accepts food with his own hand from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and eats it.'"
That bhikṣu, having gone out to the midst of the Saṃgha, should confess his transgression, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I have committed an offense that requires confession, which was not proper for me to do."
"I now repent before the Venerable One.
This is called the method of repentance.
"If a bhikṣu eats at the home of a layperson..."
If there is a bhikṣuṇī therein who points out, saying, "Give soup to so-and-so," "Give rice to so-and-so," and having given it, gives it again,
the bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister!..."
"Wait a moment; wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating.
If not even a single bhikṣu speaks to that bhikṣuṇī in this way, the bhikṣus should express their remorse, saying:
"Venerable ones! [We have committed an offense]."
"I have committed an offense that is subject to confession, which ought not to have been done.
I now confess my transgression before the Venerable One.
This is called the method of confession.
"If there are families that are under formal disciplinary action by the Sangha,
and if a bhikṣu, knowing them to be such families, accepts food with his own hands and eats it without having first received an invitation and while not being ill."
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have committed an offense that requires confession; I now confess it before you, Venerable sir."
This is called the method for repentance.

"If a bhikṣu, while staying in an araṇya that is a place of doubt and fear, does not receive food outside the monastery grounds, but instead receives food with his own hands and eats it inside the monastery grounds when he is not ill; [he commits an offense]."
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have committed an offense that requires confession, which was not proper for me to do."
"I now repent before the Venerable Ones.
This is called the method of repentance.
"Venerable Ones!..."
"I have already explained the four dharmas of confession.
Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it is asked three times. "The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter, for they remain silent; thus I shall hold this to be so."
"Venerable sirs!
These rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma) are recited every half-month from within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra:
'One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe too high.'"
"One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe too low.
One should train oneself to wear the inner robe neatly.
One should train oneself not to wear the inner robe like an elephant's trunk."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear the inner robe with tula leaves tucked in.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear the inner robe with a ball of flour tucked in.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear the three robes too high.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not wear the three robes hanging down.
One should train oneself: 'I shall wear the three robes neatly and properly.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not look left and right while wearing the robes, except for the purpose of adjusting them so they are neat.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the houses of laypeople with upright conduct.
One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the houses of laypeople with well-covered body.
One should train oneself: 'I shall enter the houses of laypeople in silence.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson while looking left and right.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit down in the house of a layperson while looking left and right.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the home of a layperson with an arrogant air.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the home of a layperson with hands on hips.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the home of a layperson with the robe draped over only one shoulder.'"
"One should train oneself not to enter the homes of laypeople with one's robe tucked up over the back.
One should train oneself not to enter the homes of laypeople while laughing or joking.
One should train oneself not to enter the homes of laypeople with the head or face covered."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson while squatting.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with hands clasped behind the back.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson by leaping.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with swinging arms.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson shaking my head.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson swaying my body.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I will not enter the house of a layperson with hands clasped.
One should train oneself: 'I will not enter the house of a layperson with feet propped up.
One should train oneself: 'I will not enter the house of a layperson with the body leaning against something.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not enter the house of a layperson with my shoulder leaning against another's.
One should train oneself: 'I shall enter only when invited.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not lie prostrate.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall sit observing the seat.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit with the body drooping heavily.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sit with the thighs crossed.'"
"One should train oneself not to sit with legs dangling.
One should train oneself not to sit with legs spread wide.
One should train oneself not to sit with legs crossed over one another."
"One should train oneself to receive food with right mindfulness.
One should train oneself not to let the bowl overflow while eating.
One should train oneself not to stretch out one's hand to seek food before it has been brought to one."
"One should train oneself: 'One must not cover the soup with rice in order to obtain more.
One should train oneself: 'One must not cover the rice with soup.
One should train oneself: 'Unless one is ill, one must not seek food for oneself.'"
"One should train oneself to receive the soup with a focused mind.
One should train oneself to receive the soup with a bowl held level.
One should train oneself not to make noise while chewing food."
"One should train oneself not to blow on food with the mouth.
One should train oneself not to eat by smelling the food.
One should train oneself not to spit upon the food."
"One should train oneself not to make a noise while eating.
One should train oneself not to protrude the tongue while eating.
One should train oneself not to bite off half a morsel of food."
"One should train oneself not to eat by pinching off leaves.
One should train oneself not to lick the hands while eating.
One should train oneself not to lick the bowl while eating."
"One should train oneself not to hold food with the hand while eating.
One should train oneself not to speak while eating from the bowl.
One should train oneself not to pull at cakes while eating."
"One should train oneself not to form the shape of a stūpa when eating.
One should train oneself not to make food into large balls.
One should train oneself not to make food into small balls."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not speak while eating. One should train oneself:
'I shall not open my mouth wide in expectation of food. One should train oneself:
'I shall not look at the bowl of a fellow practitioner and give rise to a mind of dissatisfaction.'"
"One should train oneself not to splash water on one's neighbor.
One should train oneself not to hold a water vessel with soiled hands.
One should train oneself not to discard wastewater at the residence of a layperson, unless one has asked the host's permission."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not place the alms bowl on the ground.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not wash the alms bowl while standing.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not place the alms bowl in a precarious or dangerous location.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not wash my bowl in a precarious place.
One should train oneself: 'If another person is seated and I am standing, I shall not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'When another is lying down and one is standing, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'When another is lying down and one is sitting, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself thus: 'If another person is seated while I am not seated, I must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself thus: 'If another person is in front while I am behind, I must not preach the Dharma to them.'"
"One should train oneself thus: 'When others are walking ahead and I am behind, I shall not preach the Dharma to them.
One should train oneself thus: 'When others are on the path and I am off the path, I shall not preach the Dharma to them.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except in cases of illness, one shall not preach the Dharma to those mounted on horseback.
One should train oneself: 'Except in cases of illness, one shall not preach the Dharma to those in carriages.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not preach the Dharma to a person wearing wooden clogs, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'One must not preach the Dharma to a person wearing leather sandals, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who carries a staff, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who carries a sword, except when they are ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one holding a sunshade, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one wearing a cap, except when they are ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not preach the Dharma to one wearing a flower garland, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: 'One must not preach the Dharma to one wearing a jeweled crown, except when they are ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to a person with their head wrapped, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to a person with their head covered, except when they are ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, one must not stand while defecating or urinating.
One should train oneself: 'Except when ill, one must not defecate, urinate, spit, or discharge nasal mucus into water.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not void excrement, urinate, spit, vomit, or discharge blood upon living grass.
One should train oneself: 'One must not climb trees taller than a person, except when there is a cause for fear.'"

These seven methods for settling disputes are derived from the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month.
"If a dispute arises among the bhikṣus, it should be settled and extinguished."
"Where the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) should be granted, the *saṃmukhavinaya* shall be granted.
Where the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) should be granted, the *smṛtivinaya* shall be granted."
"One for whom the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of sanity) is appropriate should be granted the *amūḍhavinaya*.
One for whom the *pratijñākāraka* (verdict by confession) is appropriate should be granted the *pratijñākāraka*.
One for whom the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (verdict based on the original statement) is appropriate should be granted the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*."
"One should grant the *yadbhūyaiṣīya*; one shall grant the *yadbhūyaiṣīya*.
One should grant the *tṛṇaprastāraka*; one shall grant the *tṛṇaprastāraka*.
O Venerable Ones!"
"I have already explained the seven methods for settling disputes.
Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter?
Thus he asks three times. "The Venerable Ones are pure in this matter, because they remain silent; thus it shall be held."

"Venerable sirs! I have already recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; I have already recited the four pārājika rules; I have already recited the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa rules; I have already recited the two aniyata rules; I have already recited the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules; I have already recited the ninety pāyattika rules; I have already recited the four pratideśanīya rules; I have already recited the śaikṣa rules; and I have already recited the seven adhikaraṇa-śamatha rules."
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as it has come down from within the Pratimokṣa Sūtra recited every half-month.
"If there are further other teachings of the Buddha, one should study them all in accordance with them, in harmony and joy, without dispute:
'In the world of the northeast, the Most Victorious One,
Honored Among Two-Legged Beings— difficult to see and difficult to encounter— has proclaimed this code of liberation.'"
Wealth is not a lasting companion; it is what the foolish delight in.
Wisdom can extinguish suffering, and at the end of life, there is constant peace and happiness.
These are the words of the Seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as they spoke the Sūtra of the Precepts for Liberation.
Those who can revere with their hearts shall obtain the unsurpassed Dharma.
Why is the precept-sūtra recited? Why is the poṣadha purified?
It is for the sake of training in accordance with the precepts, just as a wild ox cherishes its tail.
Having recited this precept-sūtra, may all the merit therein cause the sentient beings of the three realms to be entirely at peace and secure;
may they enjoy abundance and constant tranquility, and may sweet rains fall in season.
Practicing and making offerings to the Buddha, one causes the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
Now I recite the Sūtra of Precepts; who among you can hear it, receive it, and practice it?
You, the fourfold assembly and your retinues, shall thus attain peace and cross over to a happy salvation.
The World-Honored One, God among Gods, is peerless in all things;
with palms joined in ten fingers, I pay homage with head and face in a heart of reverence.
Having recited the Sūtra of the Precepts for Liberation, the Saṃgha has completed the Poṣadha ceremony.
